stem: After decomposing a task into sub-tasks, one sub-task's output is found to be incorrect while the other three are correct. What is the main practical advantage this decomposition provides at this point?

options.text: The entire task must be restarted from scratch regardless of decomposition
The agent can retry or fix just the single failing sub-task without discarding the three correct ones
Decomposition guarantees the failing sub-task will fix itself automatically
The three correct sub-tasks become invalid as soon as one sub-task fails

explanation.why_correct: This is exactly the practical benefit decomposition provides: since the sub-task results are tracked separately, only the failing one needs to be retried or fixed, preserving the already-correct work from the others.

why_incorrect.C: Decomposition does not cause automatic self-correction; a failing sub-task still needs to be explicitly retried or fixed by the agent or process.
why_incorrect.D: The correct sub-tasks' results remain valid; one sub-task's failure does not retroactively invalidate the others' already-correct outputs.
why_incorrect.A: Needing a full restart regardless of decomposition would defeat the whole point of decomposing in the first place -- isolating and preserving correct partial work is the key benefit.

explanation.rule_of_thumb: Decomposition's practical payoff shows up exactly in this kind of partial-failure scenario: fix only what's broken, keep what already works.

stem: A team applies tree-of-thought exploration to a task with no genuine branching ambiguity (every step has one clearly correct next move). What is the most likely outcome?

options.text: Dramatically improved accuracy that could not be achieved any other way
Wasted computation exploring and evaluating branches that provide no real benefit, since there was no genuine ambiguity to resolve
The task becomes unsolvable
The approach automatically converts itself into plain chain-of-thought

explanation.why_correct: Without genuine branching ambiguity, there's nothing meaningful for tree-of-thought's extra exploration to resolve -- the computation spent generating and evaluating alternative branches provides no real benefit over simply following the one correct path.

why_incorrect.A: Without genuine ambiguity, there's no accuracy gain to be had from exploring branches that all converge on the same obvious correct step.
why_incorrect.C: The task remains solvable; the inefficiency is in wasted computation, not in making the problem impossible.
why_incorrect.D: There's no mechanism by which tree-of-thought automatically reconfigures itself into a different reasoning pattern; the mismatch simply results in inefficiency.

explanation.rule_of_thumb: Applying tree-of-thought to a task with no genuine branching ambiguity wastes computation without a corresponding accuracy benefit.

stem: Which practical combination best describes how coarse upfront planning and fine-grained interleaved reasoning-action can be used together, rather than as mutually exclusive opposites?

options.text: Plan at a coarse level upfront, then interleave finer-grained reasoning and action within the execution of each planned step
Only one of the two patterns can ever be used in a single system
Interleaving must completely replace all upfront planning in every system
Upfront planning must always ignore any results obtained during execution

explanation.why_correct: A common practical combination is coarse upfront planning for overall structure, with finer-grained interleaved reasoning and action used to handle the details of executing each individual planned step.

why_incorrect.B: The two patterns are not mutually exclusive; many practical systems combine them at different levels of granularity.
why_incorrect.C: Interleaving does not need to fully replace upfront planning -- they can coexist, each handling a different level of the overall process.
why_incorrect.D: Ignoring execution results would defeat the purpose of re-planning; well-designed upfront planning does incorporate execution feedback when needed.

explanation.rule_of_thumb: Coarse upfront planning and fine-grained interleaving are complementary, not mutually exclusive -- many systems combine both at different levels.

stem: Which of the following are reasonable criteria for deciding WHERE to split a complex task during decomposition? (Select 2)

options.text: Natural sub-problem boundaries where parts of the task can be meaningfully separated and independently verified
An arbitrary fixed number of pieces chosen without reference to the task's actual structure
Points where sub-results can be checked for correctness before being combined
Splitting purely to make the total response as long as possible

explanation.why_correct: Good decomposition splits along natural, meaningfully-separable sub-problem boundaries and at points where intermediate correctness can actually be checked, both of which produce genuinely useful sub-tasks.

why_incorrect.B: An arbitrary fixed split count that ignores the task's actual structure can produce poorly separated, hard-to-verify sub-tasks rather than genuinely useful ones.
why_incorrect.D: Maximizing response length is not a meaningful decomposition criterion and has no bearing on whether the split improves verifiability or error recovery.

explanation.rule_of_thumb: Split tasks along natural, independently verifiable sub-problem boundaries -- not by arbitrary counts or to inflate length.

stem: Which task characteristic most strongly favors using plan-and-execute with decomposition over a single, non-decomposed approach?

options.text: The task has no verifiable intermediate results of any kind
The task is trivially simple with a single obvious step
The task has several clearly separable, mostly independent sub-goals
The task must be completed in under one second

explanation.why_correct: Having several clearly separable, mostly independent sub-goals is exactly the structural property that makes decomposition and planning worthwhile, since each sub-goal can be meaningfully handled and verified on its own.

why_incorrect.B: A trivially simple, single-step task has nothing meaningful to decompose, making decomposition unnecessary overhead rather than a benefit.
why_incorrect.D: An extremely tight time budget would generally argue AGAINST the added planning/coordination overhead of decomposition, favoring a faster, more direct approach instead.
why_incorrect.A: If there are no verifiable intermediate results at all, one of decomposition's key benefits (independent verification) cannot be realized.

explanation.rule_of_thumb: Separable, mostly independent sub-goals are the clearest signal that decomposition and planning will pay off.
